title: Gravlax
subtitle: scandinavian cured salmon with dill
excerpt: Gravlax is a Scandinavian classic of salmon cured in sugar, dill and seasoning. No heat is needed; the cure does all the work over 48 hours. Serves 6 as a starter.
sourceNotes: Gravlax has been made across Scandinavia for centuries, originally by fishermen who buried salted salmon in the ground to ferment. Today the method uses sugar and dill without burial.

recipe.makeAheadNotes: Make at least 48 hours ahead. The cured salmon keeps in the fridge for up to 5 days.

glossaryTerms.definition: Preserving food by drawing out moisture using sugar or salt.
Scandinavian cured salmon buried in sugar, dill and seasoning.

content.text: is one of the simplest luxury dishes you can make. A thick salmon fillet is packed in a cure of sugar, dill and seasoning, then left in the fridge for two days. What comes out is silky, deeply flavoured fish that slices like smoked salmon but has a fresher, cleaner taste.
draws moisture out of the fish and firms the flesh while the dill and sugar infuse every layer. Use the freshest salmon you can find and make sure it has been frozen first if you plan to eat it raw.
Weigh the sugar on digital scales. Mix it with the lemon zest and dill in a bowl.
Lay a large sheet of cling film in the rectangular baking tin. Place the salmon skin-side down on the cling film.
Pack the sugar and dill mixture over the flesh side of the salmon, pressing it in firmly so it covers the whole surface.
Wrap the salmon tightly in the cling film. Place another tin or board on top and weigh it down with cans. Refrigerate for 48 hours, turning the parcel every 12 hours.
Unwrap and scrape off the cure. Rinse briefly under cold water and pat dry. Slice thinly at an angle, leaving the skin behind. Serve with bread or crispbread.

attrs.problem: The salmon is still very soft after 48 hours.
attrs.solution: Make sure the parcel was weighted down. Press more firmly and leave another 12 hours. The cure needs pressure to firm the flesh.

attrs.problem: The cure looks very liquid after a day.
attrs.solution: That is normal. The liquid is drawn-out moisture from the fish. Keep the parcel sealed and turn it so the brine stays in contact with the flesh.
Rinse the cured fish more thoroughly under cold water before slicing. The surface sugar is the sweetest part.

content.text: Gravlax is eaten across Sweden, Norway and Denmark. It appears on smorgasbord tables at Christmas and midsummer. Thin slices go on dark rye bread with mustard and dill sauce. It is a centrepiece dish that takes almost no active effort to make.
